newsitem.title: GERMANY: German communists face fight over party future.
newsitem.headline: German communists face fight over party future.

text.p: Gregor Gysi, charismatic parliamentary leader of Germany's reform communists, faces a bruising battle this weekend in his bid to steer the party out of the wilderness and into mainstream politics.

Gysi is widely credited with single-handedly saving the party after the 1990 collapse of the East German communist state it ruled for 40 years. But internal battles between reformers and Stalinists rage on and the main parties keep their distance.

Gysi says he may leave politics if hardliners block his efforts to establish the Party of Democratic Socialism (PDS) as a party of power, at least on a regional level. A three-day congress in the northeastern city of Schwerin beginning Friday may prove decisive in a brief but stormy political career.

"I have come to the realisation that I don't need this job," Gysi, the highest profile member of the party's leadership team, told this week's Stern magazine. "I can become a lawyer again. I have a family and don't need all this anymore."

Although small in number, the Marxist wing of the PDS, known in its days of omnopotence as the SED, has succeeded in keeping the party debating a fundamental question: will the PDS stay true to its communist origins or will the reformers win and move it nearer the centre and closer to power?
"If we want to change society, then we have to work together with the Greens and the Social Democrats," Gysi said, referring to Germany's two main opposition parties.
"Show me with your votes that this is what you want," Gysi said he plans to tell the conference.

Although virtually non-existent in western Germany, the PDS is the third strongest party in the east. There, it portrays itself as the champion of citizens who feel Bonn fails to understand the pain of switching from socialism to capitalism.

The PDS is currently polling between four and six percent of the national vote, but it is supported by almost 20 percent of eastern voters. The PDS won 4.4 percent in the last general elections in 1994.
"I hope and am convinced that the party conference in Schwerin will send a signal that the PDS is not a foreign body but instead an important part of society," Gysi said.
"To be politically competent, we have to be in a position to offer concrete alternatives to the ruling politicians in our country and we have to be prepared to work with other (parties)," he said.
But the PDS's Marxist hardliners have rejected any cooperation with other parties.

Although the SPD and Greens have largely ruled out cooperating with the PDS on the national level, the successors to Erich Honecker's SED have helped the SPD and Greens maintain a minority government in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.

Even with Gysi's undeniable vote-winning charm and sparkling on-camera wit, the PDS will likely remain ostracised in the west for a long time. SPD and Green leaders in Bonn regularly insist they will not rely on the PDS to win power.
The hardline Marxists in the PDS, led by the photogenic Sarah Wagenknecht, would welcome Gysi's departure.

Wagenknecht, an activist in her twenties whose goods looks and dark hair swept back in a bun are reminiscent of the legendary German communist Rosa Luxemburg, says the PDS would commit political suicide by having anything to do with capitalist forms of government.
